director.chapterArc: A survivalist confrontation escalating from observation to tactical realization, culminating in a violent physical defense followed by an immediate shift to rescue. The narrator must maintain clinical distance during Jab's internal analysis but allow the pacing to tighten as the threat becomes active.
director.restraintNote: The horror of the hounds is conveyed through their stillness and unnatural behavior rather than gore or panic. Jab's exhaustion should underpin every action; he does not fight with adrenaline, but with desperate competence born of sixteen days of survival.

cues.delivery: Internal conflict: Jab's instinctive identification as 'wolf' is immediately corrected by memory. The voice should shift from a primal recognition to a cold, authoritative correction.
cues.from: Wolf, said the part of him that had grown up four hundred miles north of here, and then, immediately, in his father's voice: no it isn't.
cues.through: He had seen wolves. Wolves in the home valley did not come to a person on a road, and if they did they came apologising, sideways, with their tails and their ears making a speech about it the whole time. This one was not making a speech. It stood in the ditch side-on to him, absolutely still, from lope to stillness with nothing in between, and it did not look at him so much as it stood there being aimed at him.
cues.reason: Distinguishes the internal thought process of fear versus learned knowledge.

cues.delivery: The action is desperate but executed with practiced muscle memory. The 'shout' should be a raw noise of intimidation that fails to land.
cues.from: Jab did the thing he knew. There was no other thing to do, so he did the one from home, and it was not a stupid thing to do: he made himself big. He put his shoulders back and raised the blade up and out so the light went wide, and he took two whole steps forward, and he shouted at it — the flat carrying bark his aunt on the smoking side used on the dogs at the racks, a noise with no word in it at all, the noise that had turned every animal he had met in seventeen years.
cues.reason: Captures the physical exertion and failure of Jab's initial defense strategy.

cues.delivery: Jab's voice is unnervingly level. The narrator should strip away the panic to show Jab forcing himself into a state of functional calm.
cues.from: "Right," said Jab. His voice came out of him very level and did not feel like his. "Right. All right."
cues.reason: Highlights the dissociation and control required for survival.

cues.delivery: The realization is a hard mathematical fact. The delivery should be flat and definitive, emphasizing the impossibility of his situation.
cues.from: He could not do both. That was the whole of it, and it arrived in him complete, in one piece, with no argument attached: you cannot carry him and stand in front of him at the same time.
cues.through: So he looked for the corner.
cues.reason: Marks the pivot from panic to tactical problem-solving.

cues.delivery: Jab is speaking urgently but with absolute clarity. The tone must convey the necessity of his actions without breaking into panic.
cues.from: "Yes." He was already going to his knees beside the wall, and the whole of it had begun to happen very fast and very slowly at once. "You're going in the corner and I'm going to stand in front of you, and I can't do that with you on my back. That's the whole reason. There isn't another one."
cues.through: He got the belt buckle. It took two hands and it took four seconds and he spent every one of those four seconds with his head up, looking over the coping, at the shapes standing in the road behind him doing nothing at all.
cues.reason: Establishes Jab as a protector making difficult choices for Tonk.

cues.delivery: The scream is described with visceral weight. The narrator should slow the rhythm to let the horror of the injury and Jab's guilt land.
cues.from: He had to take the ankle strap and the thigh strap and the chest band in an order that did not matter any more, and he had to take the leg off the rail without the forearm under the calf and the elbow under the knee, because he had one hand for that and the other was holding the frame off the boy while it tipped. The rail dragged. The leg went through an angle it had not gone through since the gravel bar, and Tonk screamed — the raw full scream, the one Jab had heard twice in his life and would hear in his sleep for the rest of it — and kept screaming while Jab got both arms under him and lifted him bodily off the ground and put him down in the angle of the wall on the dead grass.
cues.reason: Emphasizes the physical cost of the rescue operation.

cues.delivery: Jab is giving orders to a terrified child. The voice should be firm but intimate, grounding Tonk in the moment.
cues.from: "Cord. Look at it. You pull that and I'm there. That's all it's ever meant and it means it now." He got the wooden fish off the stone where it had fallen and put it into the other hand, and Tonk's fingers closed on it so hard the knuckles went white. "Now. Here's your job, and it's a real one."
cues.through: "There's people down the road with lamps. Four hundred paces. When you see them coming you shout, and you shout the whole time and you don't stop, and don't you dare stop because you think I'm busy." Jab put his forehead against his brother's forehead for exactly as long as he could afford, which was one second. "Arms in. Eyes wherever you like."
cues.reason: Shows Jab's dual role as protector and commander.

cues.delivery: The realization is a cold shift in perspective. The narrator should strip away the fear to reveal Jab's sudden clarity about what he is facing.
cues.from: None of them was looking at him. They were all looking past him, at the corner, at the small shape in the dark behind his legs, and Jab understood with total clarity that they had not been counting him at all. They had been counting the thing he was carrying. They had been counting it for two miles, up a road, by the smell of an open wound and a fever at the top of its arc.
cues.through: Something happened in his chest that was not fear, although the fear was still there underneath it, running.
cues.reason: Marks the turning point where Jab understands the enemy.

cues.delivery: A single word of defiance. The delivery should be sharp and decisive.
cues.through: He stepped forward off the corner.
cues.reason: The moment Jab commits to his flawed but necessary plan.

cues.delivery: Jab's realization that the light is a barrier. The pacing should slow to let the tactical shift sink in.
cues.from: It was not a retreat. That was what took him so long to understand, standing there with his blade out and his heart going. They did not back away and they did not break. They slid — the nearest one first and then the rest, all of them at the same speed, the way a flock of birds turns without anybody deciding — round to his right, away from the lit edge, out along the fan toward the open road and the top of the ditch.
cues.through: Toward the four feet of dead grass the frame was not across.
cues.reason: Clarifies Jab's new understanding of the hounds' behavior.

cues.delivery: The collision is sudden and violent. The narration should feel physical, conveying the impact through rhythm.
cues.from: He felt the whole event through the bones of his arm: not a cut, a collision, the shoulder of something heavy running onto a held edge at speed and the edge going in and the weight coming through after it. His arm folded. His elbow hit the stone. The blade came out somewhere and the hound went past him and into the frame and through it — through it, splitting the ash lattice with a crack like a shot — and Tonk shrieked in the corner.
cues.through: Jab got his feet under him with no memory of deciding to.
cues.reason: Captures the climax of the physical struggle.

cues.delivery: The disintegration is visceral and strange. The narrator should describe the ash with a sense of unnatural finality.
cues.from: Not the way a deer came apart. It came apart all at once and from everywhere, the entire animal letting go of being an animal, and what had been a hundred and something pounds of something under his hands was a grey blowing weight of ash that went through his fingers and up his sleeves and into his mouth and eyes, and Jab knelt in the gap in a cloud of it, coughing, retching, with the blade still lit in his fist.
cues.reason: Emphasizes the supernatural nature of the enemy's defeat.

cues.delivery: Jab notices his injury with detached calm. The delivery should be flat and observational.
cues.from: His left forearm had a hole in it.
cues.through: His right hand was still holding the blade and the light was still on and the light was costing him and he could feel exactly what it was costing, which was the last of a bucket that had been nearly empty since a night in the snow.
cues.reason: Highlights Jab's exhaustion and dissociation from pain.

cues.delivery: Jab is assessing the situation with a new plan. The voice should be steady and focused.
cues.from: That was the whole of the plan and it took him about a second to arrive at, and it was the only ground on the road that mattered: four feet of dead grass with the bank at his left shoulder, the broken frame at his right, and his brother in the angle of the wall behind his heels. He stood in it with the blade lit and his left arm hanging and four hounds standing out on the crown of the road in front of him, and he had no idea at all what to do next.
cues.reason: Marks Jab's transition from defense to offense.

cues.delivery: The girl's voice is a sharp interruption. The delivery should be clear and urgent, cutting through the silence.
cues.from: "That's the light! That's where they've gone! Five went past me up the west ditch four minutes ago and I said so twice!"
cues.through: "That's the light! That's where they've gone! Five went past me up the west ditch four minutes ago and I said so twice!"
cues.reason: Signals the arrival of help and shifts the scene dynamic.

pauses.after: It was thirty feet away and a little below him, down on the slumped shoulder where the ditch began, and it was long in the body and short in the leg and the colour of wet ash. The head was a heavy wedge carried low. That was all he could see, and he could only see that much because the amber line on his fist put a wash of light out to about there and no further, and because the animal had a way of taking the light that was wrong. It did not shine and it did not go dull. The light came off its back with a shiver in it, the way air shivers over a hot stone, except that the shiver was in the animal and not in the air.
pauses.reason: Scene turn: The description of the hound's unnatural appearance requires a breath for the listener to process the horror.
Emphasizes the unnatural behavior of the hound.
Prepares for the internal correction that defines Jab's training vs. instinct.

Highlights the specific sound of intimidation he uses.
Tactical shift: The failure of his intimidation tactic needs space for Jab's mind to reset and find a new approach.
Major realization: 'Five minutes was too long.' This is the arithmetic of survival; requires weight before moving to his physical limitations.

pauses.reason: Logical pivot: The conclusion that he cannot do both tasks. A moment of forced clarity in a chaotic situation.
Emphasizes the critical tactical constraint Jab has identified.
Stresses the finality of his decision to separate from Tonk's frame.
Prepares for the visceral description of Tonk's pain and Jab's guilt.
Emotional landing: Jab's internal apology to his brother after the traumatic extraction. The pause allows the weight of 'the worst thing' to land.

pauses.reason: Instructional beat: After giving Tonk a job and a tool (fish), Jab needs a moment to ensure the child understands before he leaves him.
Emphasizes the immediate necessity of the cord for Tonk's safety.

The single word that triggers his fatal error; needs isolation.

Highlights Jab's vulnerability despite his tactical success so far.
